source: Written for this build. The situations are ordinary ones; the ORDER they should be answered in is the Financial Order of Operations (data/foo_rules.json), which is what makes a 'should have' computable rather than an opinion.
confidenceNote: Every money figure is a plausible instance, not a measurement. Scenarios are a teaching device: the point is the ORDER of the choices, not the size of the numbers.
note: DD-024. A scenario is a situation with three options. Each option carries: `serves` — the FOO step it advances, or null; `lever` — which of the seven class levers it pulls, or null; `subStats` — what practising it trains; and `money` — the deltas, each expressed as `cents` (absolute), `months` (x monthly expenses) or `pctIncome` (x gross annual income) so a scenario fits any character. The 'should have done' is NOT authored here: the engine computes it from `serves` against your live FOO placement, so it moves as you move.

rules.note: boardSize scenarios are offered each round and you resolve one — choosing what to face is itself a decision. roundsPerChapter rounds make a chapter, and a chapter ends in a review. stackWarnCount: that many of a chapter's choices on one lever raises the stacking warning. stackSubStatShare: one sub-stat taking that share of a chapter's training raises it too.

scenarios.title: The boiler gives up
scenarios.setup: It is February. The boiler makes a noise it has not made before, and then no noise at all. The engineer wants eight hundred, today.
scenarios.prompt: Where does the eight hundred come from?

options.label: Put it on the card
options.outcome: It is warm again by evening. The balance is eight hundred higher and the rate is 22%.
options.note: This is what a starter fund exists to prevent, and why it is step one.

options.label: This is what the fund is for
options.outcome: You move eight hundred and feel almost nothing. That feeling is the entire product.

options.label: Shower at the gym until March
options.outcome: You save the eight hundred and lose six weeks of evenings. The boiler still needs fixing in March, and the part has gone up.
options.note: Deferral is not avoidance. The bill waits, and sometimes grows.

scenarios.title: Eleven of them
scenarios.setup: You export a year of the current account and sort by merchant. There are eleven recurring charges. You can name four.
scenarios.prompt: What do you do with the other seven?

options.label: Cancel seven, keep four
options.outcome: Ninety-one a month back, permanently, for forty minutes of clicking. The best hourly rate you will earn this year.

options.label: Cancel the worst one
options.outcome: Fourteen a month. You feel virtuous and the other six renew on the 3rd.

options.label: You use them, sort of
options.outcome: You might. The Subscription Slime divides quietly; nobody ever signs up for eleven of anything.
options.note: Two more will appear by summer. They always do.

scenarios.title: The enrolment window
scenarios.setup: Two weeks to pick your benefits. The default is pre-ticked and someone in HR has clearly never read it.
scenarios.prompt: How much of the form do you actually read?

options.label: Read all of it, once
options.outcome: Ninety minutes. You find the match, the HSA, and a life policy you are paying for twice.

options.label: Take the defaults
options.outcome: The defaults are set for the company's convenience, not yours. Nothing bad happens today.

options.label: Miss the window
options.outcome: Enrolment closes. You are on the standard plan for a year, whichever one that is.
options.note: A year is a long time to pay for a plan nobody chose.

scenarios.title: Into the overdraft, again
scenarios.setup: Third month running. It is never much and it is always the same week.

options.label: Build a one-month buffer first
options.outcome: You cut hard for two months to get a float in place. The overdraft stops happening because it cannot.

options.label: Call and ask them to waive it
options.outcome: They waive two of the three. Pleasant, useful, and it changes nothing about next month.

options.label: Move payday around it
options.outcome: You are now managing a timing problem forever, in your head, for free.
options.note: The Overdraft Gremlin charges you for not having money — the problem you already had.

scenarios.title: The destination fortieth
scenarios.setup: Your oldest friend turns forty in Lisbon. Flights, four nights, and a dinner someone has already booked.
scenarios.prompt: Twelve hundred you have not got. What happens?

options.label: Go, and put it on the card
options.outcome: It is a wonderful weekend. It is also twelve hundred at 22%, which is a wonderful weekend and then eighteen months.

options.label: Go for the Saturday only
options.outcome: Four hundred. You are at the dinner, which was the point, and home before the expensive part.

options.label: Send a good message and stay
options.outcome: You are not there. He understands, mostly. You keep four hundred and a small ache.
options.note: Real, and the campaign will not pretend it costs nothing.

scenarios.title: Free money, declined
scenarios.setup: The employer matches the first 5%. You are putting in 2%, and have been for three years.
scenarios.prompt: What do you do with the three points?

options.label: Go to 5% from next payslip
options.outcome: A 100% return, instantly, on the only trade in finance that is actually free. Take-home drops less than you feared because of the tax.

options.label: Go to 3.5%, see how it feels
options.outcome: Half the free money. Better than none, and you will not revisit it for two years.

options.label: You need the take-home
options.outcome: Sometimes true. Three years of an unclaimed match is not a small number, and it compounds.
options.note: The rulebook calls this leaving the match on the table. It is FOO step two for a reason.

scenarios.title: The raise lands
scenarios.setup: Six percent, effective next month. It is the first real one in four years.
scenarios.prompt: Where does it go before you get used to it?

options.label: Nowhere in particular
options.outcome: By the third month you could not say where it went. The Lifestyle-Creep Hydra grows a head, and every head was reasonable.

options.label: Raise the contribution by the same six
options.outcome: You never see it, so you never miss it. This is the single highest-leverage moment a raise ever has.

options.label: Half to the future, half to now
options.outcome: Three points saved, three points enjoyed. Defensible, sustainable, and honest about being a person.

scenarios.title: Four thousand at twenty-two percent
scenarios.setup: It accumulated over two years in pieces small enough that none of them felt like a decision.

options.label: Highest rate first, hard
options.outcome: Eight hundred and eighty a year in interest, stopped. Nothing else you can buy returns 22% guaranteed.

options.label: Minimums, and get to it later
options.outcome: The minimum is designed to keep you there. At this rate 'later' is roughly nineteen years.
options.note: Debt Burden level 1: disadvantage on CON saves. It is the rulebook's own rule.

options.label: Move it to a 0% deal
options.outcome: Eighteen months of breathing room and a 3% fee. Genuinely useful — if you use the eighteen months.
options.note: A 0% card is a card with a deadline.

scenarios.title: Your sister asks
scenarios.setup: Fifteen hundred. She is good for it, probably, and has been good for it before, twice, slowly.

options.label: Give it, and call it given
options.outcome: The money is gone and the relationship is not. Nobody is owed anything, which is the cheapest possible version of this.

options.label: Lend it, with a date on it
options.outcome: Written down, a date, no interest. It works or it does not, and either way you both know which.

options.label: Say no, kindly and early
options.outcome: The hardest option and often the right one. The Well-Meaning Family Familiar is a CHA save for a reason.

scenarios.title: Eleven percent on a car
scenarios.setup: Two years left. The car is fine. The rate is not.

options.label: Overpay it into the ground
options.outcome: Every hundred is a guaranteed 11%. There is no fund that offers you that.

options.label: Refinance to six
options.outcome: Twenty minutes of forms for half the rate. Boring, unglamorous, and one of the best-paid hours available.

options.label: Actually, trade up
options.outcome: A newer car, a longer term, a bigger balance. The Commission Churn-Wraith would like a word.

scenarios.title: The rumour
scenarios.setup: Two teams went last quarter. Nobody has said anything about yours, which is exactly what they said last time.
scenarios.prompt: What do you do with the next three months?

options.label: Build the fund like it is a job
options.outcome: You get to five months. Nothing happens. That is what a good outcome looks like, and it feels like nothing.

options.label: Update the CV and take two calls
options.outcome: Not money, but Strength. The Layoff Reaper does not damage the balance — it removes the thing refilling it.

options.label: It is probably fine
options.outcome: It is probably fine. The Reaper attacks at +7 against an Armour Class you have not built.

scenarios.title: Nine thousand at nought point one
scenarios.setup: The emergency fund is doing its job. It is doing it in an account paying 0.1% while inflation does 3.

options.label: Move it to a proper savings account
options.outcome: Twenty minutes for roughly four hundred a year, every year, at no risk. Nothing else on this list is that clean.

options.label: Leave it, it is the safe option
options.outcome: It is the familiar option. The Inflation Wraith does 1d4 a month and never announces itself.

options.label: Put it in the market instead
options.outcome: Higher expected return, and no longer an emergency fund. You have swapped your armour for a bigger sword.
options.note: An emergency fund that can fall 30% on the day you need it is not one.

scenarios.title: Two thousand, one summer
scenarios.setup: The fund is at two months. The trip is real, booked-able, and with people you will not easily gather again.

options.label: Go, in full
options.outcome: It is a good holiday. The fund is still two months and you knew that when you booked.

options.label: Go, but at half
options.outcome: Same people, fewer nights, a worse hotel nobody remembers. You keep a thousand and lose almost nothing that mattered.

options.label: Finish the fund first
options.outcome: You are not there. The fund reaches four months in November and the next trip is not a decision at all.

scenarios.title: The account nobody explains
scenarios.setup: High-deductible plan, HSA offered. Everyone treats it as a medical current account.

options.label: Max it and invest the balance
options.outcome: Deductible going in, growing untaxed, out untaxed for medical. It is the only account that does all three, and it is on step five.

options.label: Use it for this year's costs
options.outcome: Fine, and a waste of the best tax shelter available to you. It is a retirement account wearing a plaster.

options.label: Too complicated
options.outcome: The Whole-Life-Insurance Basilisk thrives on exactly this: complexity as a defence against being examined.

scenarios.title: April, and the space unused
scenarios.setup: You can still fund last year's Roth for another eleven days. Seven thousand of space, permanently gone after that.

options.label: Max it
options.outcome: Never taxed again, ever. Roth space is use-it-or-lose-it and does not roll forward.

options.label: What you can — two thousand
options.outcome: Two thousand of permanently tax-free space claimed. Five thousand of it expires quietly on the 15th.

options.label: Next year
options.outcome: There is no next year for this year's space. It is the one deadline in personal finance that does not negotiate.

scenarios.title: Five thousand, once
scenarios.setup: It lands in March, taxed hard, and it is not part of your normal life.

options.label: Straight into the tax-advantaged space
options.outcome: It never becomes part of your baseline, which is the whole trick with money that arrives once.

options.label: The car, finally
options.outcome: A better car and a higher baseline: insurance, tax, tyres. The one-off became a monthly.

options.label: Half invested, half spent on purpose
options.outcome: Deliberate, spent on something chosen rather than absorbed. This is what a sustainable version looks like.

scenarios.title: A real jump
scenarios.setup: Eighteen percent and a title. It is the biggest single change to your income you will see for years.
scenarios.prompt: What does the eighteen percent do?

options.label: Fill the tax-advantaged space first
options.outcome: You max the 401(k) for the first time. Your take-home barely moves and your future changes shape.

options.label: Move somewhere nicer
options.outcome: Rent up, commute changed, and the raise is fully spent before the first payslip clears. The Rent Spike is a permanent raise to the cost of existing.

options.label: Max the space, then move
options.outcome: Both, in order. It takes eleven months instead of one and you arrive with the space filled.

scenarios.title: Twenty-five thousand and a difficult week
scenarios.setup: It arrives at the worst possible time to make a good decision, which is how it always arrives.
scenarios.prompt: What do you do in the first month?

options.label: Park it in cash for ninety days
options.outcome: You do nothing on purpose. The single best move available, and the only one that costs nothing to reverse.

options.label: Invest the lot on Monday
options.outcome: Historically the higher-expected-value move, and a genuinely hard one to hold through a bad month.

options.label: Ten for the kitchen, the rest invested
options.outcome: Named, bounded, and done deliberately. Money that arrives once should buy something you can point at.

scenarios.title: Your colleague is up three hundred percent
scenarios.setup: He tells you at lunch, twice. He has told everyone. He is not lying.

options.label: Put five thousand in
options.outcome: The Crypto Siren does not chase you — that is the whole trick. It sings the number you needed to hear.

options.label: A hundred, as a toy
options.outcome: Bounded, named as entertainment, and it cannot hurt you. Most people cannot actually hold this line.

options.label: Nothing, and change the subject
options.outcome: Market Literacy negates this one outright. You know what a returns figure quoted without a time period is worth.

scenarios.title: The thing that takes all of it
scenarios.setup: You have a house, a car, savings, and a teenager about to drive. One bad afternoon reaches all of it.
scenarios.prompt: What stands between that afternoon and everything?

options.label: Buy the umbrella policy
options.outcome: Two hundred a year for full plate against the single biggest possible hit. Armour Class, not judgment.
options.note: +3 AC in the rulebook's own terms.

options.label: Raise the deductibles instead
options.outcome: Cheaper premiums, more exposure. You have made the common hits worse to make the rare one no better.

options.label: It will not happen to you
options.outcome: It probably will not. The Medical Bankruptcy Behemoth attacks at +8 and does 12d10.

scenarios.title: If you could not work on Monday
scenarios.setup: Your income is one body. There is a group policy at 40% and a private one that would take it to 65.
scenarios.prompt: What do you do about the gap?

options.label: Top it up privately
options.outcome: Forty a month to protect the entire Strength column. The Sudden Ability Drain is an attack roll, and this is the armour against it.

options.label: The group policy is fine
options.outcome: Forty percent of your income, taxed, if the definition is met. Read the definition.

options.label: Nothing, for now
options.outcome: The one that protects your income directly, declined. It is the most-skipped armour on the sheet.

scenarios.title: Down thirty-four percent
scenarios.setup: Eleven months of gains, gone in six weeks. Every headline agrees it is different this time.
scenarios.prompt: What do you do on the worst Tuesday?

options.label: Nothing. Deliberately nothing.
options.outcome: The crash was a paper loss and cost you nothing. The panic-sell is the damage, and you did not take it.

options.label: Move it to cash until it settles
options.outcome: You crystallise the loss and now need to be right twice. 8d10 weeks is what selling at the bottom costs a real pile.

options.label: Buy more, on schedule
options.outcome: Same contribution, cheaper units, no heroics. The Market Crash Elemental is a WIS save and you made it.

scenarios.title: Three point one percent
scenarios.setup: Fourteen years left. You have five hundred a month spare and two obvious homes for it.

options.label: Overpay the mortgage
options.outcome: A guaranteed 3.1%, tax-free, and a house owned outright sooner. Worse on a spreadsheet, better in a bad decade.

options.label: Invest it
options.outcome: Higher expected return over fourteen years, and a mortgage that is still there in the bad decade.

options.label: Half each
options.outcome: The answer most people can actually hold, which makes it better than the optimal one they abandon.

scenarios.title: The flat downstairs
scenarios.setup: The maisonette below comes up. You could buy it, live in half, and let the other.

options.label: Buy it and let the other half
options.outcome: Your housing cost is hedged by a tenant. It is the House Hack feat, and it is +1 AC in the rulebook's terms.

options.label: Run it properly, then decline
options.outcome: The numbers do not work at this price. Declining after doing the work is a skill, not a failure.

options.label: Buy property the liquid way instead
options.outcome: Property exposure without the tenant, the boiler, or the concentration. Less upside, far less to go wrong.

scenarios.title: Forty percent in one ticker
scenarios.setup: Years of vesting have quietly made your employer your largest holding. They also pay your salary.
scenarios.prompt: What do you do about the concentration?

options.label: Sell down to ten percent
options.outcome: You pay some tax and remove the case where one company takes both your income and your savings on the same day.

options.label: It has been good to you
options.outcome: The Concentration Golem is built from a single stock, usually your employer's, usually while it was working.

options.label: Stop buying more, keep what you have
options.outcome: You stop adding without triggering the tax. Half a fix, and it stops the problem growing.

scenarios.title: Vesting in eighteen months
scenarios.setup: You do not like the job. Leaving costs a number you can compute exactly, which is what makes it hard.
scenarios.prompt: What do you do with the eighteen months?

options.label: Work out the real number and decide
options.outcome: You price the years, not just the equity. The Golden Handcuffs' damage is the years, not the money.

options.label: Stay for the vest, obviously
options.outcome: Eighteen more months. It may well be right — it is only a trap if you never did the sum.

options.label: Leave now
options.outcome: You walk from real money for real reasons. Expensive, and sometimes the only way out.

scenarios.title: Your mother needs help
scenarios.setup: Not a crisis. A slow one: appointments, then afternoons, then most of a week a month.

options.label: Money and time, split with your brother
options.outcome: Named, shared, and written down before anyone is exhausted. The Care-Giving Toll takes income and hours at once.

options.label: Send money, keep the job
options.outcome: Cleanest financially. Somebody else is still doing the afternoons, and it is usually the nearest sibling.

options.label: Drop to four days
options.outcome: Twenty percent of your Strength, given deliberately. The right call for many people and it should be a decision, not a drift.

scenarios.title: Six months off
scenarios.setup: You have the runway. You have not had more than eleven consecutive days off in nine years.

options.label: Take the six months
options.outcome: Your pile stops growing and starts justifying itself. This is what tier IV is for — working out what it was for.

options.label: Take two months
options.outcome: Most of the reset, a fraction of the cost, and no conversation with anyone about a gap on a CV.

options.label: Not yet
options.outcome: There is always a reason. Tier IV's own note: the question stops being how much and starts being when, and then why.

scenarios.title: You crossed it in March
scenarios.setup: What you have already invested will fund the retirement you want, without another penny added.

options.label: Take the interesting job that pays less
options.outcome: The pile carries the retirement; the salary only has to carry today. This is the option Coast FI buys and almost nobody takes.

options.label: Keep going, retire earlier
options.outcome: Entirely legitimate. Worth checking, once, that it is a choice and not a habit wearing the clothes of one.

options.label: Stop entirely
options.outcome: Coast is not Full. The difference is roughly a decade of expenses, and the Sequence-of-Returns Serpent lives in the first five years.

scenarios.title: Two hundred a month, from nothing
scenarios.setup: The thing you built at weekends now earns without you touching it most weeks.
scenarios.prompt: What do you do with it?

options.label: Put six months into scaling it
options.outcome: The Builder's whole lever: income created from nothing rather than negotiated from someone.

options.label: Feed it back in, slowly
options.outcome: It grows at the speed it grows. No second job, no burnout, and it is still there in two years.

options.label: Take it as spending money
options.outcome: Two hundred a month of pure lifestyle, and the thing stays exactly the size it is.

scenarios.title: The ad that knows
scenarios.setup: It followed you here. Money in your account in ten minutes, it says, and it is not lying.

options.label: No — write down what the £200 was actually for
options.outcome: It was a car repair you knew about in March. The list is short and it is the same list every year, which means it can be saved for.

options.label: Ask someone you know instead
options.outcome: Cheaper than the ad by a very long way. It also spends something you cannot rebuild as easily as money.

options.label: Take the ten-minute money
options.outcome: You have it by lunchtime. The fee is a flat number that looks small and is an annual rate you would not say out loud.
options.note: This is the Overdraft Gremlin with a marketing budget: it charges you for not having money.

scenarios.title: Four percent
scenarios.setup: Your first raise. It lands in the account on the 28th and it is genuinely nice.

options.label: Straight into the starter emergency fund, before you see it
options.outcome: You never adjust to it, so you never miss it. The float is finished months earlier than it would have been.

options.label: Half to the fund, half to your life
options.outcome: Slower, and you actually keep doing it. A rule you follow beats a rule you abandon in March.

options.label: Upgrade the flat
options.outcome: The raise is now a permanent bill. Raises can be taken back by a landlord more easily than by an employer.
options.note: Lifestyle creep is the only monster that arrives on your best day.

scenarios.title: A refund you forgot about
scenarios.setup: Nine hundred pounds you had already mentally spent on nothing in particular.

options.label: It is the emergency fund, finished
options.outcome: The one job a windfall is unambiguously good at: buying a floor you did not have.

options.label: Onto the credit card
options.outcome: Right money, wrong rung — with no float, the next surprise puts it straight back on the card.

options.label: Take it, and fix why it happened
options.outcome: A refund is your own money, returned late and without interest. You change the code so next year it arrives monthly instead.

scenarios.title: Your flatmate is moving out
scenarios.setup: Six weeks' notice, politely given. Your share of the rent is about to be all of it.
scenarios.prompt: What do you do with the six weeks?

options.label: Find someone before they go
options.outcome: Boring, unglamorous, and it keeps a fixed cost cut in half. Fixed costs are the ones that decide how hard everything else is.

options.label: Use the break to move somewhere cheaper
options.outcome: A month of upheaval buys a permanently lower floor. Moving is one of the few levers that changes the monthly number and stays changed.

options.label: Cover it alone and see how it goes
options.outcome: It goes the way the arithmetic says. The gap does not close by being lived in.
options.note: This is the fixed-cost share of your spending rising — the number Constitution is built out of.

scenarios.title: The second property
scenarios.setup: A flat two streets over, priced like someone needs it gone this month.
scenarios.prompt: Is this the thing to do with the money?

options.label: Price it properly — voids, repairs, management, tax — then decide
options.outcome: The honest yield is well under the headline once a month of voids a year is in it. You may still buy, but not by accident.

options.label: Put the deposit in the index fund you already hold
options.outcome: No tenants, no boiler, no second mortgage. Less of a story to tell and about the same expected return.

options.label: Buy it — it is cheap and it will not be there next week
options.outcome: You are now a landlord with one tenant, which is a portfolio of one. When they leave, your income from it is zero.
options.note: Concentration is the risk here, not property. One tenant is not diversified.

scenarios.title: Which pot first
scenarios.setup: The income has stopped on purpose. Three pots, taxed three different ways, and a number you need each year.
scenarios.prompt: Which one do you draw from first?

options.label: Work out the order once, on paper, and follow it
options.outcome: Drawing in the right order is worth years of spending at the far end, and it costs one afternoon. It is the highest-paid afternoon of the whole plan.

options.label: Hold two years in cash and refill it in good years
options.outcome: You stop being forced to sell into a fall. It costs a little return to buy the ability to not care what the market did this year.

options.label: Take it from whichever account is easiest to reach
options.outcome: Convenient, and it quietly hands years of the plan to the tax code. Nothing feels wrong at any single withdrawal.
options.note: The damage here is invisible per-transaction and enormous cumulatively, which is what makes it worth a rule.

scenarios.title: Thirty-nine a month, forever
scenarios.setup: The handset is 'free'. The contract is two years and the maths is done somewhere you cannot see it.

options.label: Keep the old handset, take a rolling SIM
options.outcome: The handset was never free — it was a loan at a rate nobody had to print. You keep the difference every month, and you can leave any time.

options.label: Ring them and say you are leaving
options.outcome: Ten minutes of mild discomfort takes a third off. The number was always negotiable; nobody was ever going to volunteer that.

options.label: Sign — it is only thirty-nine a month
options.outcome: Two years at thirty-nine is nine hundred and thirty-six pounds, committed, for a phone. Small monthly numbers are how large annual ones get past you.
options.note: This is the fixed-cost share creeping up — the number Constitution is built out of.

scenarios.title: The review
scenarios.setup: Good ratings, warm words, and no number mentioned anywhere in forty minutes.

options.label: Ask for a number, out loud, before you leave the room
options.outcome: Ninety uncomfortable seconds. They say they will look into it, and because you asked, they do. Nobody has ever been given a raise for being obviously excellent and silent.

options.label: Find out what the job pays elsewhere first, then ask
options.outcome: Three ads and one honest coffee. You go in with a figure rather than a feeling, and the figure is higher than the one you would have asked for.

options.label: Wait for the pay round. It's only a few months.
options.outcome: The pay round applies a percentage to the number you already have. You have just agreed to be raised from the wrong starting point.
options.note: Waiting is a decision. It is usually the expensive one.

scenarios.title: Someone else is offering
scenarios.setup: A recruiter you did not chase. The number is meaningfully higher and you like your team.
scenarios.prompt: What do you do with it?

options.label: Take it
options.outcome: Changing employer still moves pay more than being excellent where you are. Unfair, thoroughly documented, and true.

options.label: Show your boss and ask them to match
options.outcome: They match about half of it. You keep the team, and you are now the person who has one foot out — which cuts both ways for years.

options.label: Turn it down quietly and say nothing
options.outcome: Loyalty is lovely and it is not a financial instrument. You have priced yourself and told nobody, including yourself.

scenarios.title: The first pound
scenarios.setup: You have a skill people ask you about for free. Regularly.
scenarios.prompt: Does anyone ever pay for it?

options.label: Charge someone. Anything. Once.
options.outcome: The gap between nothing and one pound is the entire distance. Everything after that is volume, and volume is the easy part.

options.label: Spend a weekend making it into something you can actually sell
options.outcome: A page, a price, a way to pay. Slower off the line and it keeps earning while you are asleep.

options.label: Keep doing it for free. It's only ever a favour.
options.outcome: Genuinely fine. Just know that you now have no answer to the question of what you would do if the job stopped on Friday.
options.note: Hustle Capacity is not about the money. It is about having an answer.

scenarios.title: Money or the title
scenarios.setup: They will give you one of the two this year and they are being unusually honest about it.

options.label: The title
options.outcome: A title resets the band you get paid inside. A raise moves you within the one you are already in. This is slower this year and larger by the third.

options.label: The money, now
options.outcome: Real, spendable, and it compounds from today. It also leaves you in the same band next year, asking the same question.

options.label: Ask for the title now and the money at the next review, in writing
options.outcome: They say yes more often than people expect, because it costs them nothing this quarter. In writing is the load-bearing part.

scenarios.title: Three quiet years
scenarios.setup: You look back and your pay has moved about two percent a year. Inflation did not.

options.label: Call it what it is — a pay cut — and plan to fix it this year
options.outcome: Two below-inflation years in a row is a pay cut wearing a nice hat. Naming it is what makes it a problem you can act on.

options.label: Pick one thing your industry is short of and get visibly good at it
options.outcome: Visibly is doing the work in that sentence. Nobody has ever paid more for a skill they could not see.

options.label: It's a tough market. Everyone's the same.
options.outcome: Some of them are. The ones who moved are not, and in ten years the gap between you is not recoverable by working harder.

scenarios.title: Six hours a week
scenarios.setup: You have found six hours. Genuinely found them, not imagined them.

options.label: Something that pays, however badly at first
options.outcome: A second income is not really about the money at this size. It is about no longer having exactly one thing between you and nothing.

options.label: Getting better at the thing that already pays you
options.outcome: Lower variance, and it raises the number that is already the biggest one you have. Boring and frequently correct.

options.label: Rest. Actually rest.
options.outcome: Not a wrong answer. Burnout has ended more earning careers than bad investing ever has, and this game cannot score that.

scenarios.title: Naming your rate
scenarios.setup: They ask what you charge. There is a pause and it is your turn to fill it.
scenarios.prompt: What comes out of your mouth?

options.label: A number higher than feels comfortable — then say nothing
options.outcome: The silence afterwards is the entire technique. Most people fill it and negotiate against themselves before the other side has spoken.

options.label: Ask what they had budgeted
options.outcome: Sometimes a gift, sometimes an anchor dropped on your foot. Worth asking once — never worth accepting immediately.

options.label: Something safe. You want the work.
options.outcome: You get the work, and the rate you name first becomes the rate they expect forever. Raising it later is a much harder conversation than naming it now.

scenarios.title: The reorganisation
scenarios.setup: Nothing announced. But the good projects have stopped arriving and you have noticed.
scenarios.prompt: Six weeks of warning. What do you do with it?

options.label: Start talking to people now, while you still have a job
options.outcome: You negotiate far better from inside a job than outside one, and everybody on the other side of the table knows it.

options.label: Cut hard and get another month of cash in the account
options.outcome: It buys you the ability to say no to the first offer, which is usually worth more than the month itself.

options.label: Work harder and hope it passes
options.outcome: Sometimes it does. It is not a plan, it is a wish with overtime attached.

scenarios.title: Money you cannot reach
scenarios.setup: Most of what you have saved is somewhere with a penalty attached to leaving early.

options.label: Move a month of it somewhere you can actually get to
options.outcome: Money behind a penalty is not available in the week you need it, and the week you need it is the only week that counts.

options.label: Find out what it actually costs to get at, on a calm afternoon
options.outcome: Same-day, three days, or a penalty. Three very different answers, and the worst time to learn which is the bad Tuesday.

options.label: Leave it. It's earning more where it is.
options.outcome: It is. Until the day it has to be sold at whatever price the morning offers, which is precisely the day you did not plan for.

scenarios.title: Twelve months or twenty-four
scenarios.setup: The longer one is cheaper per month. Meaningfully cheaper.

options.label: Twelve. Pay the difference for the option to leave.
options.outcome: Every extra month locked in is a month you cannot take a better offer somewhere else. That option has a price and this is it.

options.label: Twenty-four. The saving is real and I'm not going anywhere.
options.outcome: Defensible if it is true. The trouble is that the offer worth moving for never arrives during a month you had planned for it.

options.label: Sign the long one, but ask for a break clause
options.outcome: They often say yes because it costs them nothing today. You get the lower rate and keep the door.

scenarios.title: What leaves whether you like it or not
scenarios.setup: You sit down and write out every payment that goes out automatically.
scenarios.prompt: What do you do with the list?

options.label: Kill the single biggest one you could live without
options.outcome: One big cut beats six small ones, and you only have to be brave the once. The list is always longer than the memory of it.

options.label: Refinance everything above about seven percent
options.outcome: The rate is the wound; the balance is only how big it is. Same debt, materially less bleeding.

options.label: Feel briefly alarmed, then file it
options.outcome: The list does not shrink from being looked at. It was never the looking that was the hard part.

scenarios.title: Remote, but only verbally
scenarios.setup: You work from anywhere. It has never been written down and your manager is leaving.

options.label: Get it in the contract before they go
options.outcome: A verbal arrangement is worth exactly nothing the day the person who agreed it walks out. This costs one awkward email.

options.label: Say nothing and hope the new one is relaxed about it
options.outcome: They might be. You have made your ability to live where you live somebody else's decision, and you will not be told when it changes.

options.label: Price what it would cost to be in the office three days a week
options.outcome: Commute, time, childcare, the lot. Knowing the number turns a vague dread into a thing you could negotiate about.

scenarios.title: The car is dying
scenarios.setup: Another repair, and the next one is not far behind it.

options.label: Something dull, paid for outright
options.outcome: No monthly payment is a permanent raise you gave yourself, and it cannot be repossessed when a bad year arrives.

options.label: Finance something newer. The monthly is manageable.
options.outcome: Manageable is doing a lot of work there. You have converted a one-off problem into a fixed cost that outlives your interest in the car.

options.label: Work out whether you need one at all
options.outcome: Sometimes the answer is genuinely no, and it is the largest single cut available to most households.

scenarios.title: Somewhere cheaper
scenarios.setup: The same life, forty minutes further out, for four hundred less a month.

options.label: Go. Four hundred a month is four hundred a month.
options.outcome: Housing is the largest lever most people will ever have and the one they touch least. Moved once, it stays moved.

options.label: Price the whole thing first — commute, time, what you'd lose
options.outcome: Forty minutes each way is roughly a working day a week. Sometimes the saving survives that and sometimes it does not.

options.label: Stay. There's more to life than the rent.
options.outcome: Completely true, and worth being deliberate about rather than default about. You are buying something with that four hundred — make sure you know what.

scenarios.title: They've made you an offer
scenarios.setup: Your first proper one. The number is written down and you are trying not to look too pleased.
scenarios.prompt: Do you say yes straight away?

options.label: Ask for a bit more. Politely, once.
options.outcome: They expected you to. Almost nobody does at this stage, and the number you start on follows you through every percentage rise for a decade.

options.label: Ask about the things that aren't salary
options.outcome: Pension match, holiday, the training budget. Cheaper for them to say yes to, and the match in particular is money you would otherwise simply not be given.

options.label: Say yes. Obviously yes.
options.outcome: Fair enough — and every rise you ever get here is a percentage of this number. Starting low is the most quietly expensive thing on this page.
options.note: Your starting salary is the base every future rise is calculated from.

scenarios.title: Overtime, if you want it
scenarios.setup: Two extra shifts a week are going spare. Not forever, but for a while.

options.label: Take them, and send every penny straight to the buffer
options.outcome: Temporary money aimed at a permanent problem. The shifts end; the month of breathing room does not.

options.label: Take them and enjoy the extra
options.outcome: Entirely allowed. Just notice that your spending will quietly rise to meet it and will not fall back when the shifts stop.

options.label: No. The time is worth more than the money right now.
options.outcome: Often the right call and almost never said out loud. Exhaustion has ended more earning careers than bad investing ever has.

scenarios.title: The course
scenarios.setup: Six weekends and about four hundred pounds. People with it earn visibly more.

options.label: Check three job ads that ask for it before paying anything
options.outcome: Five minutes that decides whether four hundred pounds is an investment or a hobby. Most courses fail this test.

options.label: Do it. It pays for itself in two months if it works.
options.outcome: One of the few things that reliably lifts the biggest number you have. It is also six weekends you do not get back.

options.label: Ask work to pay for it
options.outcome: They often will, because it is cheap for them and looks good. You have just used their budget to raise your own market rate.

scenarios.title: What you're worth a day
scenarios.setup: You have been quietly charging the same for three years and you are busier than ever.

options.label: Raise it for everyone, with a date and no apology
options.outcome: Fully booked at a rate you have not moved in three years is not success, it is a pricing error you have been paying for.

options.label: Raise it for new clients only
options.outcome: Painless, slower, and it works. Within a year the old rate is a small and shrinking part of your income.

options.label: Hold it. They've been loyal.
options.outcome: Loyalty runs both ways and they are not offering you a rise unprompted. Being fully booked is the market telling you the price is too low.

scenarios.title: Salary or equity
scenarios.setup: They will pay you well, or slightly less and a slice of the thing.

options.label: Take the salary. Equity in most companies is worth nothing.
options.outcome: Statistically hard to argue with. Certain money now beats a lottery ticket you cannot sell, and you can invest the difference yourself.

options.label: Take the salary and negotiate the equity separately
options.outcome: They are two different conversations and treating them as one is how people give away the first to win the second.

options.label: Take the equity. This one's different.
options.outcome: It might be. Make sure the salary you accept is one you could live on for years, because that is the actual bet you just made.

scenarios.title: They'd like you on the board
scenarios.setup: A day a month, a fee that is not life-changing, and a room you have never been in.

options.label: Take it. The room is the point, not the fee.
options.outcome: The fee is incidental. The people in that room are where the next three opportunities come from, and you cannot meet them any other way.

options.label: Find out what you'd be liable for first
options.outcome: Directors carry duties that do not vanish because it was a favour. One afternoon of reading, before rather than after.

options.label: No. A day a month is a day a month.
options.outcome: Reasonable. Time is the thing you have least of at this stage and the only one you cannot buy back.

scenarios.title: Everything you have is the deposit
scenarios.setup: You have saved hard. All of it is earmarked for one flat.

options.label: Hold a month of expenses back, outside the deposit
options.outcome: Completing on a flat with nothing left is how a boiler becomes a credit card. The month you keep is what stops that.

options.label: All of it. A bigger deposit is a smaller mortgage.
options.outcome: True, and it leaves you owning something illiquid with no cash at all. The first surprise after moving in goes on a card at twenty-odd percent.

options.label: Wait three months and go in with both
options.outcome: Three months of slightly worse timing buys a permanently better position. Boring, and it is what people who never get into trouble do.

scenarios.title: Six months' notice
scenarios.setup: The new contract is good. The notice period is twice what you have ever had.

options.label: Ask for three. It is almost always negotiable.
options.outcome: A long notice period is a lock on your own front door held by somebody else. They will usually trade it, because it costs them nothing today.

options.label: Work out what it costs you to be stuck for six months
options.outcome: One missed offer. That is the price, and it is not small — but at least you will have chosen it rather than skimmed past it.

options.label: Sign it. It's standard.
options.outcome: It is standard, and it is still six months in which the best thing you will be offered all year cannot be accepted.

scenarios.title: Most of it is in one thing
scenarios.setup: The bulk of what you own is a single holding you cannot sell quickly or quietly.
scenarios.prompt: What do you do about it?

options.label: Sell it down slowly, on a schedule you set in advance
options.outcome: A schedule decided in a calm month is worth enormously more than a decision made in a bad one. Set it, automate it, stop watching.

options.label: Borrow against it rather than sell
options.outcome: Keeps the position and adds a lender to your life who can call at the worst possible moment. Occasionally clever, frequently how people get wiped out.

options.label: Just build a cash floor beside it and leave it alone
options.outcome: You are not trying to be optimal. You are trying to never be forced to sell it on a Tuesday you did not choose.

scenarios.title: The place you barely use
scenarios.setup: It is lovely. It is also insured, heated, maintained and standing empty most of the year.

options.label: Add up every pound it costs a year, including the ones you forget
options.outcome: Standing charges, insurance, maintenance, the tax. The honest total is usually about double the number people carry in their heads.

options.label: Let it out for the months you are not there
options.outcome: Turns a fixed cost into something that partly pays for itself, at the price of it no longer being entirely yours.

options.label: Keep it exactly as it is. That is what the money was for.
options.outcome: A completely legitimate answer, and the only one on this page that requires you to have decided it on purpose rather than by default.
